newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australia headed for near-record crop - ABARE.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australia headed for near-record crop - ABARE.

text.p: Australia's official commodity forecasting agency, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE), has forecast a near-record Australian winter crop of 28.7 million tonnes for 1996/97.

Wheat production is forecast to rise by 11 percent to 18.8 million tonnes. The combination of excellent late opening rains, relatively high cereal prices and depressed returns for wool were the main reasons for the increase in plantings, ABARE's executive director, Brian Fisher, said in a statement.
Plantings were up by seven percent, he said in a statement accompanying AGARE's latest Australian Crop Report.
Prospects for winter crops ranged from average yields in southern Australia to above average in Queensland and New South Wales, he said.
In Queensland above average rains in May provided an ideal opening to the Queensland winter crop season, he said.
Plantings in Queensland were estimated to have risen by 47 percent to nearly 1.4 million hectares.
Production in Queensland was forecast to almost triple to almost 2.3 million tonnes, although significant rain was needed over the next month to prevent possible moisture stress, he said.
A recovery in yields was expected after several consecutive below-average seasons, Fisher said.
For southern Australia, the absence of general opening rains until mid-June had led to lower plantings than expected of crops with earlier optimum planting times such as lupins and canola.
Heavy June and July rains had led to problems with waterlogging, disease and weed infestation, particularly in Western Australia, Fisher said.
Despite an increase in area overall, production in southern Australia was expected to fall in 1996/97 as yields turn to more normal levels after a good season in 1995/96, he said.
ABARE is also forecasting improved prospects for the 1996/97 summer crop season because of good subsoil moisture levels already established.
Also, the Bureau of Meteorology is forecasting potentially above average rainfall in parts of south eastern Queensland to October 1996, Fisher said.
The Australian cotton industry was no longer facing the acute shortages of irrigation water of the past four years, with dam capacity averaging 68 percent, he said.
Better water allocations would allow growers to resume irrigating crops, he said.
